extracted.intended_audience: Coast Guard contracting officers, Contracting Officer's Technical Representatives (COTRs), acquisition/contracting managers, and policymakers evaluating or administering outsourced functions under OMB Circular A-76
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and administration standards for Coast Guard functions contracted out under OMB Circular A-76 (performance expectations, contract language, oversight, cost-comparison methodology, and recommended contract provisions). Useful for people auditing, drafting, or managing such service contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response time compliance with PWS
rubrics_metrics.description: Response times by contractors should meet the performance timeframes specified in the Performance Work Statement (PWS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenants complained contractors responded slower than former government staff, although response times were generally within those specified in the PWS. Monitor actual response times against PWS requirements and consider customer expectation changes during transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of work performed
rubrics_metrics.description: Work performed by contractors should meet the quality standards specified in the contract/PWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report notes the quality of work was acceptable in studied contracts. Where quality falls below specified levels, contracts need mechanisms (see deduct/incentive provisions) to motivate corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include deduct/incentive provisions for substandard performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm fixed-price contracts should include deduct provisions and/or incentives to address and correct substandard contractor performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As written, studied contracts lacked methods to take deductions for sub-standard performance; Contracting Officers often gave second chances. Including deduct provisions provides a formal means to get the contractor's attention and improve performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and accountability for Government Furnished Equipment (GFE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts and transition plans must provide systems to maintain accountability/inventory for GFE to prevent misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools and small high-dollar items were made available to contractors but no inventory/accountability system was put in place after contract start. Perform inventories and establish GFE accountability procedures when turning over equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible and proactive Administrative Contracting Officer (ACO) support
rubrics_metrics.description: ACOs should be familiar with the contract, make site visits, and provide timely contract interpretations and administrative support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When function was managed locally earlier, the ACO visited and was familiar; centralized ACO in MLC had not visited site and provided slow/no interpretations. Recommendation: MLC should provide better contract administration and add staff as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear contract definitions to avoid disputes (e.g., 'appliances' vs 'equipment')
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts must contain clear definitions for categories (such as 'appliances' vs 'equipment') to avoid differing interpretations between Government and contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disagreement over whether water heaters are appliances (Government replacement) or equipment (contractor replacement); contractor's written request for clarification went unanswered. Contracting Officers should issue timely written clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for delivery lead times of GFE/Government Furnished Material (GFM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract language and schedules must account for long transit times/distance-related delays in delivery of GFE/GFM to locations like Hawaii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late arrival of GFE/GFM caused schedule slippages and cost increases. Contractors/Government should plan logistics and schedule buffers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly specified roles and authorities for Housing Officer/COTR and other officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties, authorities, and points of contact for the Housing Officer, assistant Housing Officer, and COTR must be specified to eliminate contractor confusion about who has authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor reported multiple Housing Office personnel tasked activities but uncertainty about actual authority; specifying individual responsibilities reduces misunderstanding and disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal written designation and training of COTRs
rubrics_metrics.description: COTRs should be formally designated in writing by the Contracting Officer and receive proper training (not just on‑the‑job).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some contracts the COTR had not been designated in writing and interviewees reported no formal training. Recommendation: provide formal training programs and written designations for COTRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive Performance Work Statement (PWS) to reduce disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive, detailed PWS reduces the need for clarifications and disputes between Government and contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where PWS was comprehensive (e.g., Support Center Seattle), few problems arose and little clarification was necessary. Identified minor PWS problems should be corrected before re-solicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include special-event requirements in the PWS (e.g., dignitary meals)
rubrics_metrics.description: PWS should explicitly address infrequent but mission-important events (such as meals for visiting dignitaries) and how they are to be handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galley contract lacked guidance on serving visiting dignitaries; command preference conflicted with contractor meal counting. Including such requirements lets contractors plan and price appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment method tied to measurable outputs and included pricing schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts should specify payment methodology tied to measurable outputs (e.g., meals served) and include schedules/prices used to calculate payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Food services contract paid monthly based on actual numbers of meals and included a schedule of meal prices; this clarity supported accurate billing and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate Department of Labor (DOL) wage determinations and adjustment mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts must incorporate applicable DOL wage determinations and provide for equitable price adjustments or modifications when prevailing wages change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wage determination adjustments were the primary drivers of contract cost increases; contracts were modified to reimburse contractors for increased wages. Include DOL determinations and adjustment clauses to handle retroactive/retro adjustments and equitable price adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and manage contract modifications and change orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect and plan for contract modifications (extensions, wage adjustments, additional work, accounting changes); provide processes for handling change orders and delivery orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studied contracts had numerous modifications (extensions, wage determinations, added work). Contract files should document each modification and its impact on price and schedule; where possible handle additional work via delivery orders rather than change orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous cost-comparison methodology for MEO vs contract price
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing contractor vs government (MEO), calculate government costs using current GS/WG/military pay scales, convert WG hours (2,087 hours/year), include retirement and FICA, BAQ/BAS for officers, and use consistent assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis used GS/WG pay scales, 2,087 hours/year, retirement estimated at 29.15% of base pay, FICA at 7.15%, and included allowances; this methodology showed contractors remained more economical despite wage increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for capital improvement add-on when returning to in‑house performance
rubrics_metrics.description: If returning a function to in-house performance, include a 25% increase for capital improvements when computing government costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government estimate would automatically be increased by 25% for capital improvements, making return to in-house performance more costly; factor this into decisions about reverting functions to government performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-monetary impacts before outsourcing further
rubrics_metrics.description: Before contracting out more functions, study and understand non-monetary impacts (loss of flexibility, reduced shore-rotation opportunities, loss of training opportunities for personnel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary savings were evident, but the report recommends further study of unknowns such as effects on flexibility, careers, and training, which are not captured in simple cost comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer contracting for routine work that is well-detailed in the PWS
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions that are routine and are specified in detail in the PWS tend to have fewer problems when contracted out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support Center Seattle's guard services (routine and detailed in PWS) had successful contractor performance and few disputes; use detailed PWS for routine, repeatable services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use SBA 8(a) set‑aside mechanisms appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: For eligible functions, contracting under the SBA 8(a) set-aside program for small/disadvantaged businesses is an appropriate procurement mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the report include use of SBA 8(a) set-aside for Group San Diego food services and other functions; contracting officers negotiated prices under that program.
